## Import and inspect the SPSS data

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(labelled)
library(gt)
library(psych)
```

```{r}
#| label: import-inspect
data_raw <- read_sav("data/Case31.sav")

dim(data_raw)
names(data_raw)
glimpse(data_raw)
summary(data_raw)
```

### Initial data questions

1.  How many rows and columns are in the imported data? The SPSS file contains 128 respondent records and 34 variables. Each row represents one record and each column represents one variable.

2.  What are the variable names? I print all names above. The survey items are `q3` through `q27`, `q30` through `q34`, `q37`, and `q38`. The file also contains `OverallEmployeePerformace` and `employeeperformance`, which appear to be previously calculated employee-performance variables. The exact names can be checked in the output from `names(data_raw)`.

3.  Which variables are questionnaire items and which are precomputed? Variables beginning with `q` and followed by a number correspond to structured questions in the questionnaire. The two employee-performance variables are not individual questions. I exclude them from the working questionnaire dataset so I can evaluate the employee items myself.

4.  Variable labels versus value labels. A variable label describes what a question measures, such as "Employees are courteous." Value labels explain the numbers used to record the response, such as `1 = Strongly disagree` and `5 = Strongly agree`.

5.  Which variables contain missing values? The table below identifies missing values in the imported file. Q7, Q8, and Q37 contain missing values; the original file also includes code `3 = No answer` for Q12, which needs to be handled separately because it may still appear as a numeric value.

```{r}
#| label: missing-raw
missing_raw <- data_raw |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  filter(n_missing > 0)

missing_raw |> gt()
```

## Create a data dictionary

The data dictionary records each variable's name, descriptive label, type, observed distinct values, and coded value labels. It is useful because an SPSS file contains label information that is not always visible in the data frame.

```{r}
#| label: dictionary-raw
data_dictionary <- tibble(
  variable = names(data_raw),
  variable_label = map_chr(data_raw, \(x) attr(x, "label", exact = TRUE) %||% ""),
  class = map_chr(data_raw, \(x) class(x)[1]),
  n_distinct = map_int(data_raw, n_distinct),
  value_labels = map_chr(
    data_raw,
    \(x) {
      labs <- attr(x, "labels")
      if (is.null(labs)) "" else str_c(labs, "=", names(labs), collapse = "; ")
    }
  )
)
data_dictionary |> gt()
```

### Data dictionary questions

Which labels are clear, and which need improvement? Employee statements Q3–Q6 are recognizable, but several existing SPSS labels are shortened or generic. Q8 incorrectly repeats a statement-frequency label even though it asks about borrowing rates. I correct it to "Opinion about rates charged on borrowed funds." The precomputed variables should also be distinguished from original survey questions.

Measurement levels. Q11 (whether statements are understandable), Q27 (whether a member currently has a credit union loan), and Q38 (living in the headquarters area) are nominal yes/no variables. Q7 and Q8 are ordinal rate judgments because their categories have an order. Q13–Q26 are coded awareness/use categories; the professor also asks us to consider treating them as ordered for a recoding exercise, although they are not an equal-interval attitude scale. The Q3–Q6 and Q30–Q34 five-point agreement questions are ordered single items, but the instructor treats them as approximately scale/interval for reliability, factor analysis, and computing an index.

Which value labels are essential? The awareness/use categories and the special codes "No opinion" and "No answer" require explicit labels. The agreement scale is more predictable, but its intermediate categories also need labels so the report is readable. For example, some raw items initially label only the two endpoints of the 1–5 scale.

## Improve variable and value labels

The questionnaire provides the coding instructions. I add all five agreement labels, fix the borrowing-rate label for Q8, and supply the full labels for awareness, yes/no, and overall management ratings. Labelling is not a recode: numeric values do not change in this section.

```{r}
#| label: metadata
agreement_labels <- c(
  "Strongly disagree" = 1, "Disagree" = 2, "Uncertain" = 3,
  "Agree" = 4, "Strongly agree" = 5
)
rate_labels <- c(
  "Very high" = 1, "High" = 2, "Average" = 3,
  "Low" = 4, "Very low" = 5, "No opinion" = 6
)
frequency_labels <- c(
  "Too often" = 1, "Very often" = 2, "About right" = 3,
  "Not often enough" = 4, "Never" = 5
)
accuracy_labels <- c("Excellent" = 1, "Good" = 2, "Fair" = 3, "Poor" = 4)
yes_no_labels <- c("Yes" = 1, "No" = 2, "No answer" = 3)
awareness_labels <- c(
  "Aware and have used" = 1,
  "Aware but have not used" = 2,
  "Unaware" = 3
)
overall_labels <- c(
  "Excellent" = 1, "Good" = 2, "Average" = 3,
  "Poor" = 4, "Very poor" = 5, "No answer" = 6
)

data_labelled <- data_raw |>
  set_variable_labels(
    q8 = "Opinion about rates charged on borrowed funds",
    q37 = "Overall rating of credit union management and operations"
  ) |>
  set_value_labels(
    q3 = agreement_labels, q4 = agreement_labels,
    q5 = agreement_labels, q6 = agreement_labels,
    q30 = agreement_labels, q31 = agreement_labels,
    q32 = agreement_labels, q33 = agreement_labels,
    q34 = agreement_labels,
    q7 = rate_labels, q8 = rate_labels,
    q9 = frequency_labels, q10 = accuracy_labels,
    q11 = yes_no_labels, q12 = yes_no_labels,
    q27 = yes_no_labels, q38 = yes_no_labels,
    q13 = awareness_labels, q14 = awareness_labels,
    q15 = awareness_labels, q16 = awareness_labels,
    q17 = awareness_labels, q18 = awareness_labels,
    q19 = awareness_labels, q20 = awareness_labels,
    q21 = awareness_labels, q22 = awareness_labels,
    q23 = awareness_labels, q24 = awareness_labels,
    q25 = awareness_labels, q26 = awareness_labels,
    q37 = overall_labels
  )

val_labels(data_labelled$q33)
val_labels(data_labelled$q13)
var_label(data_labelled$q8)
val_labels(data_labelled$q37)
```

### Adding, editing, and removing labels

The `labelled` package can read a variable label with `var_label()` and coded responses with `val_labels()`. In the code above I use `set_variable_labels()` and `set_value_labels()` to replace incomplete metadata. To demonstrate label removal without damaging the real dataset, I make a temporary copy below.

```{r}
#| label: label-demonstration
q8_example <- data_labelled$q8
var_label(q8_example)
val_labels(q8_example)

q8_example <- remove_var_label(q8_example)
q8_example <- remove_val_labels(q8_example)
var_label(q8_example)
val_labels(q8_example)
```

The questionnaire's Exhibit 31.2 shows that Q7 and Q8 use code 6 for No opinion, but Q37 uses code 6 for No answer. Q11, Q12, Q27, and Q38 use the yes/no convention with code 3 for No answer. These codes should not contribute to ratings or indexes.

## Create a questionnaire-only analysis copy

I remove the two precomputed employee-performance variables from the working dataset. Using a precomputed index would skip the reliability and factor checks that this assignment is meant to practice. I keep the questionnaire variables only, as the professor demonstrates.

```{r}
#| label: analysis-copy
data <- data_labelled |>
  select(matches("^q\\d+$"))

names(data)
```

## Data-quality and missing-value checks

I compare numeric codes against the response options in the questionnaire. The original paper responses are not provided, so I cannot confirm whether repeated answers reflect inattention. I do not delete any cases solely because several ratings are the same. The case narrative mentions 125 returned questionnaires and two exclusions, while the supplied SPSS file contains 128 records; I cannot establish why these counts differ.

```{r}
#| label: quality-checks
data |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") |>
  summarise(
    values_observed = str_c(sort(unique(value)), collapse = ", "),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    pct_missing = round(mean(is.na(value)) * 100, 1),
    .by = variable
  ) |>
  gt()
```

No observed numeric codes appear outside the options in Exhibit 31.2. The imported data already contain missing entries for Q7, Q8, and Q37, and Q12 has a code 3 for "No answer" that must not be treated as a substantive yes/no response. This verifies the supplied electronic data; the completed paper questionnaires are not available for individual checks.

### Recode "No opinion" and "No answer" as missing

`read_sav()` uses `user_na = FALSE` by default, which can already convert SPSS-defined missing codes to `NA`. I also explicitly recode the questionnaire's special codes to ensure they do not remain as valid responses. The value labels remain attached to the variables.

```{r}
#| label: special-missing
sum(as.numeric(data$q7) == 6, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(as.numeric(data$q8) == 6, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(as.numeric(data$q37) == 6, na.rm = TRUE)

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    across(c(q7, q8, q37), ~ na_if(.x, 6)),
    across(c(q11, q12, q27, q38), ~ na_if(.x, 3))
  )

data |>
  select(q7, q8, q12, q37) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  gt()
```

All 128 supplied records are retained provisionally. The dataset can reveal missing and out-of-range codes, but it cannot establish whether every original questionnaire was genuinely completed by an attentive member.

## Reverse-code selected questions

The original rating direction is higher numerically for less favorable answers on Q10 and Q37. Reversing these makes larger scores represent a more positive evaluation. Q7 and Q8 are also reversed for consistency of the numeric rate *level*, but a higher borrowing rate is not necessarily a better outcome.

```{r}
#| label: reverse-ratings
data <- data |>
  mutate(
    q7r = 6 - as.numeric(q7),
    q8r = 6 - as.numeric(q8),
    q10r = 5 - as.numeric(q10),
    q37r = 6 - as.numeric(q37)
  ) |>
  set_variable_labels(
    q7r = "Savings-rate opinion, reversed (higher = higher perceived rate)",
    q8r = "Borrowing-rate opinion, reversed (higher = higher perceived rate)",
    q10r = "Statement accuracy, reversed (higher = better)",
    q37r = "Management and operations, reversed (higher = better)"
  ) |>
  set_value_labels(
    q7r = c("Very low" = 1, "Low" = 2, "Average" = 3, "High" = 4, "Very high" = 5),
    q8r = c("Very low" = 1, "Low" = 2, "Average" = 3, "High" = 4, "Very high" = 5),
    q10r = c("Poor" = 1, "Fair" = 2, "Good" = 3, "Excellent" = 4),
    q37r = c("Very poor" = 1, "Poor" = 2, "Average" = 3, "Good" = 4, "Excellent" = 5)
  )
```

### Why Q9 is different

Why should Q9 not be reversed? Q9 asks how often statements arrive, with "About right" in the middle. Neither "Too often" nor "Never" is necessarily better. A calculation such as `6 - q9` would only reverse the order, not represent satisfaction.

To answer "was the frequency about right?", I would use code 3 to identify respondents who chose "About right" and compare their frequency with the other responses. This keeps the original five response categories intact.

### Awareness items Q13–Q26: hypothetical ordinal recoding

Q13–Q26 record whether someone has used a service, knows of it but has not used it, or does not know about it. These are meaningful categories, not a 1–3 satisfaction measure. I would normally summarize them with separate frequencies or percentages, not average them into one satisfaction index.

However, the new instructions specifically ask us to suppose they are treated as an ordinal awareness/use scale and reverse-code them. The following creates separate illustrative columns where `1 = Unaware`, `2 = Aware but not used`, and `3 = Aware and have used`.

```{r}
#| label: awareness-example
data <- data |>
  mutate(across(q13:q26, \(x) 4 - x, .names = "{.col}r")) |>
  mutate(across(q13r:q26r, \(x) add_value_labels(
    x,
    "Unaware" = 1,
    "Aware but have not used" = 2,
    "Aware and have used" = 3
  ))) |>
  set_variable_labels(
    q13r = "Regular share accounts (reversed awareness)",
    q14r = "Special subaccounts (reversed awareness)",
    q15r = "Christmas club accounts (reversed awareness)",
    q16r = "Individual retirement accounts (reversed awareness)",
    q17r = "MasterCard credit cards (reversed awareness)",
    q18r = "Signature loans (reversed awareness)",
    q19r = "New car loans (reversed awareness)",
    q20r = "Late model car loans (reversed awareness)",
    q21r = "Older model car loans (reversed awareness)",
    q22r = "Household goods/appliance loans (reversed awareness)",
    q23r = "Recreational loans (reversed awareness)",
    q24r = "Share collateralized loans (reversed awareness)",
    q25r = "IRA loans (reversed awareness)",
    q26r = "Line of credit loans (reversed awareness)"
  )

data |> count(q13, q13r)
```

### Verify the recodes

I compare each original question with its reversed value. Reversal should map 1 to the maximum, 2 to the next-highest value, and so on, without creating a score for missing answers.

```{r}
#| label: verify-recodes
data |> count(q7, q7r)
data |> count(q8, q8r)
data |> count(q10, q10r)
data |> count(q37, q37r)
```

## Evaluate two candidate multi-item measures

The professor identifies two possible constructs: employee proficiency (Q3–Q6) and operational effectiveness (Q30–Q34). I check both using Cronbach's alpha, corrected item-total correlations, and one-factor analysis. The statistical item sets are converted to ordinary numbers for the analysis, while the prepared questionnaire dataset keeps its metadata.

### Employee proficiency: Q3–Q6

These statements describe whether employees are courteous, helpful, professional, and available. They appear to be different aspects of one employee-proficiency concept.

```{r}
#| label: employee-reliability
employee_items <- data |>
  select(q3:q6) |>
  remove_val_labels() |>
  remove_var_label()

employee_alpha <- psych::alpha(employee_items)

employee_alpha$total
employee_alpha$item.stats[, "r.drop", drop = FALSE]
employee_alpha$alpha.drop[, "raw_alpha", drop = FALSE]
```

```{r}
#| label: employee-factor
employee_fa <- psych::fa(
  employee_items,
  nfactors = 1,
  rotate = "none",
  fm = "minres"
)

employee_fa$loadings
employee_fa$communality
```

Interpretation: Cronbach's alpha is approximately 0.866. The corrected item-total correlations are positive and the items load together on a common factor; the one-factor solution explains approximately 63% of the variance in the classroom example. All four questions relate to employee behavior, so it is reasonable to calculate a single employee-proficiency index. This is preliminary evidence of consistency, not complete proof of validity.

### Operational effectiveness: Q30–Q34

These statements concern loan rates, financial confidentiality, application speed, meeting members' needs, and ease of application. Although they are all positive statements, they reflect several different parts of credit union operations.

```{r}
#| label: operations-reliability
operations_items <- data |>
  select(q30:q34) |>
  remove_val_labels() |>
  remove_var_label()

operations_alpha <- psych::alpha(operations_items)

operations_alpha$total
operations_alpha$item.stats[, "r.drop", drop = FALSE]
operations_alpha$alpha.drop[, "raw_alpha", drop = FALSE]
```

```{r}
#| label: operations-factor
operations_fa <- psych::fa(
  operations_items,
  nfactors = 1,
  rotate = "none",
  fm = "minres"
)

operations_fa$loadings
operations_fa$communality
```

Interpretation: Cronbach's alpha is approximately 0.539, considerably lower than for Q3–Q6. The corrected item-total correlations are weaker, especially for some operational questions. They do not all appear to represent one narrow construct as convincingly as the employee questions do. I would keep Q30–Q34 as separate items rather than create a single operational-effectiveness index. The one-factor analysis is a useful diagnostic, but the meaning of the items also matters.

### Summary of the two candidate scales

```{r}
#| label: reliability-summary
reliability_summary <- tibble(
  proposed_measure = c("Employee proficiency (Q3-Q6)", "Operations (Q30-Q34)"),
  raw_alpha = round(c(employee_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
                      operations_alpha$total$raw_alpha), 3),
  index_decision = c("Create index", "Keep items separate")
)

reliability_summary |> gt()
```

## Create the justified index

Because Q3–Q6 have consistent coding, good reliability, and compatible wording, I calculate their row mean. The `na.rm = TRUE` option allows a score if some valid items remain; if all four items are missing, `NaN` is changed to `NA`. I do not create an operational-effectiveness index.

```{r}
#| label: create-index
data <- data |>
  mutate(
    employee_proficiency_index = rowMeans(pick(q3:q6), na.rm = TRUE),
    employee_proficiency_index = if_else(
      is.nan(employee_proficiency_index), NA_real_, employee_proficiency_index
    )
  ) |>
  set_variable_labels(
    employee_proficiency_index = "Employee proficiency: mean of Q3-Q6"
  )

summary(data$employee_proficiency_index)
```

The employee-proficiency index has an average of approximately 4.205 on a 1–5 scale. This suggests that members generally rated employee proficiency positively. It does not answer the case's borrowing-behavior research questions by itself; that would require later analysis.

## Data-preparation decisions and limitations

I imported the supplied SPSS file using `read_sav()` and created a data dictionary to inspect the variable names, labels, and response codes. The SPSS file contains 128 records and 34 variables, including two precomputed employee measures. I excluded those measures from my working analysis because the purpose was to evaluate the original questionnaire items independently.

I added complete response labels and corrected Q8's borrowing-rate label. For missing values, I treated Q7/Q8 code 6 as "No opinion," Q37 code 6 as "No answer," and yes/no code 3 as "No answer." I checked the codes against Exhibit 31.2 and retained the 128 records provisionally because the individual completed questionnaires were not available for verification.

I reversed Q7, Q8, Q10, and Q37 to make the numeric directions interpretable and checked the results against the original values. I did not reverse Q9, because its preferred response is in the middle. I also completed the requested hypothetical reversal of Q13–Q26 but did not treat those awareness/use categories as a single attitude scale.

Finally, I found good internal consistency for employee proficiency (Q3–Q6), so I created its mean index. The operational items (Q30–Q34) had substantially weaker consistency and broader meanings, so I kept them separate. The original case narrative and supplied SPSS file report different record counts, and the source paper questionnaires are not available to resolve the discrepancy. These are limitations of the available data, not reasons to invent exclusions.

## Confirming completeness of data wrangling

I make one more data dictionary from the prepared data to verify that the corrected labels and new variables are present. The complete check is saved with the cleaned dataset; the table below displays key variables to keep the report readable.

```{r}
#| label: final-dictionary
final_dictionary <- tibble(
  variable = names(data),
  variable_label = map_chr(data, \(x) attr(x, "label", exact = TRUE) %||% ""),
  value_labels = map_chr(data, \(x) {
    labs <- attr(x, "labels")
    if (is.null(labs)) "" else str_c(labs, "=", names(labs), collapse = "; ")
  }),
  n_missing = map_int(data, \(x) sum(is.na(x)))
)

final_dictionary |>
  filter(variable %in% c("q8", "q12", "q13", "q13r", "q37", "q37r",
                         "employee_proficiency_index")) |>
  gt()
```

## Confirm the prepared data and save the SPSS file

The final `data` object retains the original questionnaire items and their labels, the requested recoded variables, and the justified employee-proficiency index. The original `data_raw` object remains unchanged. I save the cleaned version with my initials, XL, and the required word cleaned.

```{r}
#| label: confirm-export
val_labels(data$q8)
val_labels(data$q13r)
var_label(data$employee_proficiency_index)
summary(data$employee_proficiency_index)

dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_sav(data, "outputs/XL_Case31_cleaned.sav")
file.exists("outputs/XL_Case31_cleaned.sav")
```
